decision: The driver is built in Rust (portable-pty, a vt100 screen model, rmcp for MCP), offered as a command, as scenes in CI, and as an MCP server.
rejected: Adopting a Python MCP server; driving tmux (an extra program between, and a coarser screen); screenshots and vision for terminals (heavy, and text is already there).
why: Whatever ships is Rust; the pieces exist; the Python servers found show the design.

decision: The project is called agent access.
rejected: mcp-oco (names one protocol, not the purpose); agent-bridge (vague); tui-driver (one of its parts).
why: It says the purpose plainly: every tool usable by agents.

decision: lab-agent is delivered by the package conveyor (linux-package-distribution-oco/conveyor@v1); it keeps only its declaration, build scripts, PKGBUILD, public key and install test.
rejected: Keeping its own copy of the delivery machinery.
why: Its delivery workflows were a near copy of snapall's; copies drift and fixes do not travel.

decision: lab-agent records each wait itself - start, end, what is waited on, the project - and requires both on a waiting submit; a gatherer brings the waits into each project's data.
rejected: Logging waits by hand (it would be skipped); estimating them afterwards.
why: Capture must be unavoidable and cost nothing: the place every wait happens is lab-agent's own wait.

decision: Every process a job starts carries the job's mark in its environment (OCO_AGENT_JOB). When the job ends, overstays, or was left by a run that died, everything carrying its mark is ended - asked to stop first, then made to. Something meant to outlive a job is started as a service, not as its child.
rejected: Process groups (a child can leave its group); a death signal to children (it reaches only the direct child); systemd's control group alone (tests, and machines without it, would have nothing; it still helps where present).
why: Crash-only cleanup must not trust the runner to have lived: a dead run's jobs are found by their mark and cleared before anything else happens. The mark reaches children's children, which nothing else here does.

decision: Work is asked for through the jobs repository as files under oco-agent/jobs - apart from lab-agent's jobs/, so during the switch neither agent takes the other's work. A file's top line says who asked, when and its limits, and counts only at the top. When work was asked comes from the asking, never from when it is read. Drivers' beats are the repository's Actions variables. Only oco-agent-github knows GitHub.
rejected: Taking the moment of reading as the moment of asking; a header read anywhere in the script; a separate metadata file beside each script (two writes, and a window with one but not the other); beats as commits; a second repository for oco-agent's jobs (the same trust and the same token, twice the setup).
why: An agent that was down must not see old work as new: the asking's own time makes such work expire instead of run (the quieter cousin of the 2026-11-11 replay). A header read anywhere is how lab-agent's client lost a line from inside a script. A beat every few minutes as a commit would fill the history with hundreds of meaningless commits a day.

decision: oco-agent is built inside lab-agent's repository (oco-agent/), tested by its CI and kept out of its releases, until it takes over and the repository takes its name.
rejected: A new repository now (the reasoning and the code would live apart, and the history would split).
why: Its design, research and backlog already live here; lab-agent must keep serving while it is proven; tad's Rust version grew the same way.

decision: Each driver - a person or a machine - has a lease of its own, kept alive by its beats: a job starts only while the driver who asked for it is still there. Beats are what is known now, not a history: one fact per driver, a newer beat replacing an older and never the reverse; they are kept apart from the journal, behind their own port, with their own check in the measure.
rejected: One lease for 'the' driver (the first design: a silent AI would have stopped the author's work too); beats as journal entries (hundreds of lines a day that say nothing after the next one).
why: oco-agent coordinates work for any driver; one driver going silent must not stop another's work, and must stop its own. Beats arrive often and only the latest matters, so they are state, where the journal is history.

decision: The redesigned lab-agent is oco-agent: born beside lab-agent, which serves until the switch - as tad's Rust version grew beside the Python one - then lab-agent retires.
rejected: runner (GitHub's word - true, but it says nothing of the voice, the journal or the leases); keeping lab-agent (it names a place, not what it belongs to); renaming in place (the old one must keep serving until the new one is proven).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: it is tied to ocoeco by design. 'agent' is the established word for this role; 'oco-' names its family and its dependency on ocoeco.

decision: lab-agent's core speaks its own language and depends on nothing outside itself (a crate with no input or output); every technology - git and GitHub, ntfy, systemd - is an adapter behind a port the core defines, and its words appear nowhere above it; areas are named for what lab-agent is for; the playbook's guards check it on every change; in-memory adapters run the chaos tests. The journal is declared tad tables queried with SQL, and where they live is itself an adapter; finished work becomes glimpses. The journal's SQL is tad's, and tad's SQL is DuckDB's (tad-engine 2026-11-12-sql-is-duckdb), as tad's original research decided.
rejected: A core that calls GitHub and git directly (the prototype's way, and the root of the incident's reach); folders named ports and adapters (the playbook: names say what the program is for); the journal as files in a repository with no declaration.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: follow the ideal-project guidelines; the implementation must not rely on GitHub - it is today's adapter, and switching it (to Redis, say) must be a clean replacement; git as a heap of files is a one-off mess when tad is a database and ocoeco makes every action intelligible.

decision: oco-agent is trusted with nothing until it has watched lab-agent: a shadow run reads lab-agent's newest log every ten minutes through oco-agent's rules, keeps its own journal, and alerts urgently when lab-agent starts work oco-agent would have refused. It decides; it never acts.
rejected: Switching to oco-agent at once (proven only on the past); a daily report (a replay storm ran 102 jobs in twenty minutes on 2026-11-11).
why: Rules proven on tests and on one night's log should also hold on the days that follow, before they run anything; and lab-agent is still the one running jobs, so a replay there must be noticed at once.

decision: What happened is spoken back to the repository work was asked through, on a branch of its own (spoken): the journal, and each job's log. It is written only when something changed - the journal at most every ten seconds, a running job's log at most every minute, a finished job's log at once - logs before the journal, so a driver who reads that a job ended finds its log there. Only jobs the running agent did are spoken. A driver anywhere uses standing, log and wait with --via; waiting is a beat, and wait's exit status says how the job ended (0 finished, 1 failed, 124 out of time, 3 expired, 4 parked, 2 not ended yet).
rejected: A second repository for results, as lab-agent has (two places for a driver to look, twice the setup); writing on main (the asking history drowned in reports); writing every change at once (commits by the second); speaking every log in the folder when a runner starts (a burst after each restart).
why: A driver must see how work went from wherever it drives, as with lab-agent's results - but in the one repository it asked through. The history of asking stays readable on main. Writing only on change keeps within GitHub's limits on content creation as well as its hourly budget.

decision: Everything that polls GitHub asks conditionally (ETag), so an unchanged answer costs nothing; oco-agent reads what is left of the hour's budget from every answer and, below 500, takes work in only every 2 minutes, saying so once. Writing - commits, variables - happens only when something changed.
rejected: Polling without conditions (about 480 an hour for intake alone); a fixed slower interval (slow even when the budget is plentiful); a second account or token for the agent (two secrets to keep and rotate, and the token is to be rotated already).
why: The 5,000-an-hour budget is shared by everything on the account; one careless poller can starve land, the client and the pin updater together. lab-agent had learned this; the redesign must carry it over, not lose it.

decision: oco-agent does work through Hands - start, look, stop, clear - whatever actually runs a job (processes on this machine today). A job is claimed in the journal before it starts, and does not start if the claim is refused; its end is written as it happens, and an end that could not be written is kept and written at the next step. Each job says how long it may run and is stopped if it overstays. A run of the agent is numbered by the moment it began, to the millisecond.
rejected: Starting first and writing after (a crash between the two leaves a job run and unrecorded); a counter of runs kept on disk; retrying a job that could not start (it would fail the same way, repeatedly).
why: The replay of 2026-11-11 came from work whose record lived apart from the doing; here nothing starts unrecorded. Deciding needs only that no two runs share a number, so a moment serves where a counter would be more state to keep right.

decision: The lab is watched by a dead man's switch outside GitHub: oco-agent sends its pulse to it (OCO_AGENT_PULSE_URL, or a private file ~/.config/oco-agent/pulse-url) after each healthy turn of its loop, at most every five minutes; when pulses stop the switch alerts the author through ntfy. The watcher workflow stays as a second, probing check where GitHub's schedules fire. Lives since 2026-11-12 09:44 UTC: pulses every five minutes, the check up.
rejected: Trusting GitHub's schedule (it fired not at all); a timer on the lab sending the pulse (blind to an agent that stalls while the machine runs); the lab dispatching the watcher (silent exactly when the lab is down); an outside cron calling the watcher (two moving parts where one does).
why: GitHub's schedules proved unreliable on this account: the watcher had no scheduled run at all, in a private repository and then a public one, and lab-agent's daily gather has run by schedule once in two days, hours late. A pulse from the working loop stops for every failure that matters - the machine, its network, an agent that stalls - and needs no clock of our own.

decision: lab-agent is redesigned around a journal per job, run-once by construction, the driver's lease with park-on-silence, each job's heartbeat, flows of idempotent steps that resume, a working tree per job and side-by-side by resource, crash-only recovery, a watcher outside the machine, secrets kept out of URLs, and its data flowing through ocoeco - in five stages, each proven by chaos tests before the next (DESIGN.md). Refined the same day by 2026-11-12-ports-names-and-tables: ports and adapters with the playbook's names and guards, and the journal as tad tables queried with SQL.
rejected: Patching the replay and carrying on (the other paths stay open); adopting a durable-execution engine such as Temporal or Restate (a server to run and secure on one machine with no inbound port - lab-agent takes their proven ideas into a small core instead, with git as the record it already has).
sources: temporal-durable-execution, kleppmann-locking, healthchecks, crash-only, k8s-jobs, idempotency-keys
why: The 2026-11-11 incident traced to a foundation laid as a one-off prototype; the author asked for the best the world has learned, with the full picture in mind.

decision: oco-agent takes over the running of jobs step by step, each with a way back (DESIGN.md, The switch): it serves beside lab-agent; its client ships in lab-agent's release; drivers move, the AI first; the watcher probes it; and only when it has a voice of its own does lab-agent's daemon stop. Until then lab-agent's daemon keeps running - it carries the author's notifications and the board pushed to the phone - and is simply no longer asked to run jobs. oco-agent's service keeps the lab awake while it serves.
rejected: Stopping lab-agent's daemon now (the author's notifications and board pushes would stop without a word); moving everything at once (nothing to fall back to); letting the lab sleep when idle (it is set to suspend after an hour: it would take no work and look silent to the watcher).
why: Live work, the author's phone flows, the probes and the shadow all depend on what runs today; each step must be provable and reversible on its own. The daemon's voice was found by reading it before planning to stop it.

decision: Drivers say things to one another (oco-agent say, inbox); what is said is a tad table beside the journal. A driver with a channel on this machine has it carried to their phone through ntfy - urgent words on the urgent topic - and what they answer on their own topic is heard as something they said to everyone. How each job of such a driver ended is said to them once, with its last lines. The topics live in a private file on the machine; a voice that fails rests five minutes.
rejected: Notifications as a thing apart from what drivers say (two mechanisms for one act); telling the author how every job ended (hundreds a day: only a reachable driver's own jobs - others say what matters themselves); trying a failed send again every turn; the board in this step (next: most likely the items in progress in ocoeco's data, not a list of its own).
why: It carries what lab-agent's voice had learned: two channels, so the phone can let urgent ring through; the topics' names are the secret and never leave the machine, so whoever speaks never needs them; a failed send waits, since the server counts by the day. And it is simpler: the author is a driver like any other, so one table and one way serve notifications, replies and talk between drivers.

decision: The watcher runs in this public repository (.github/workflows/watch-the-lab.yml), probes oco-agent instead of lab-agent - asking through the jobs repository as the driver 'watcher' and reading the answer from what oco-agent speaks - and counts any end of a probe as an answer. It keeps only the newest probes. Every GitHub listing oco-agent relies on is read from the git tree, and a listing cut short stops the taking-in instead of passing in silence.
rejected: Keeping the watcher in the private repository and nudging its schedule (no way to see whether GitHub registered it); an outside cron service now (another account to create - kept as the watcher's own guard, see watch-the-watcher); listing with the contents API (silently cut at 1,000).
why: In the private jobs repository GitHub never ran the watcher's schedule (0 scheduled runs, while this account's public repositories ran theirs - the observatory's at 07:10 that morning); a watcher that can stop without anyone noticing is the gap it was built to close. lab-agent is disabled after replaying; oco-agent does the work now. A listing that silently stops at 1,000 caused both replays.

decision: The lab is watched from outside by probing it: a workflow in the jobs repository asks a tiny job every half hour and alerts the urgent channel itself - once - when the lab has not answered for 45 minutes; it says so when the lab answers again, and asks no new probe while one is unanswered. It needs no secret beyond the channels: the probe writes its answer back into the same repository with the lab's own token.
rejected: A timer on the lab sending beats (blind to an agent that stalls while the machine runs); a hosted dead man's switch such as Healthchecks (one more account, and still fed by the lab); a probe every few minutes (noise in the jobs repository, and a long job would look like silence).
why: On 2026-11-11 the agent stalled while the machine was on, and the only alert path ran through the agent. A beat from a timer would have stayed happy through the stall; only work actually done proves the agent takes work (black-box probing). Watching from GitHub keeps the alert independent of the lab.

decision: A tad dataset is DuckDB's EXPORT DATABASE folder - one JSON-lines file per table - edited with SQL and brought back to canonical, diffable files; jq and Miller work on the same files.
rejected: Doltgres and Dolt (history where a pull request cannot show it); gitsheets (no SQL, no joins); GlueSQL (an engine reinvented, without ALTER TABLE); SQLite with sqlite-diffable.
sources: duckdb-spike, tad-origin-log, duckdb-export, dolt, gitsheets, sqlite-diffable
why: Everything queryable, versioned and diffable in one place; measured in the spike: a no-op round trip leaves zero diff at 200,000 rows, one changed row is one changed line.

decision: tad was extracted from a repository that already worked (the software-engineering canon), not designed first in the abstract.
rejected: Designing the template first.
why: An abstraction is right only once it has met a real case; designing first risked assumptions that would not survive real content.

decision: Each repository vendored the engine as a git subrepo at .tad/, pinned in a readable .gitrepo, one commit per sync. Superseded 2026-11-11: copies drifted (three of four older); tad is now called, not copied - released binaries, pinned per repository, moved weekly (2026-11-11-one-release-path, 2026-11-11-pins-moved-by-the-lab).
rejected: git subtree (two commits per sync, the pin buried in a commit trailer).
why: Tested against git subtree on a real update: subrepo writes one commit per sync instead of two and states the pinned commit plainly.

decision: tad is released by release-please (versions and changelog from conventional commits) with the package conveyor building binaries in the same run; the tag-triggered workflow is gone.
rejected: Tagging by hand with land --tag as the release path; keeping both paths.
why: One release path, no manual version bumps; a tag made with GitHub's own token cannot start another workflow, so the binaries are built in the same run.

decision: The lab machine moves each repository's tad pin (bin/update-pins.sh, weekly), landing through land so each repository's CI decides.
rejected: A GitHub workflow with GitHub's token (its pull requests start no CI); the author's personal token as a secret in four repositories (spreads the key); a GitHub App (the clean CI-native way - needs the author's setup; a later upgrade).
why: A pull request opened by a workflow with GitHub's own token starts no CI, so a pure-GitHub updater would open unchecked pull requests; the lab machine already holds a token and lands through checks.

decision: tad in Rust: tables declared as data (after Frictionless Table Schema); one tool - check, canonical form, row edits with a check, documents rendered from data; proven equal to the Python version on all four repositories (same verdicts, same documents) before any switch; delivered by the package conveyor instead of vendored; ocoeco's shapes become a tad declaration. The tool is delivered by the package conveyor (for CI and machines); the library is taken as a Rhizoid cutting where a project builds on it (ocoeco) - as tad's own path already says, a rhizcut in every repository. Corrected 2026-11-12 by 2026-11-12-sql-again: SQL is not optional - tad answers real SQL through an embedded SQLite.
rejected: Rust bindings to DuckDB keeping schema.sql (a database engine to validate text); Dolt (a separate store); keeping the vendored copies.
why: The author: tad stays general and Python leaves. The four schemas need no database engine: their 41 tables use only patterns, allowed values, required fields and one list column.

decision: When the four repositories switch to tad, their documents are re-rendered by today's renderer; the canon's and Rhizoid's change visibly, and that is said in the switch's own change.
rejected: Porting the older renderers too, to switch without visible change.
why: Their vendored copies are older; the switch is the first time they get today's renderer. A change people did not expect should be announced, not discovered.

decision: tad's SQL engine is a port in tad's own words (load the declared tables, run a statement, give the tables back), and its adapter today is DuckDB's pinned standalone binary, checked by fingerprint and installed beside tad; a stand-in serves the tests; an embedded DuckDB stays possible as another adapter if it ever builds statically.
rejected: Embedding DuckDB now (no static build, slow builds, a large binary).
why: Measured (carrying-duckdb): embedding costs six minutes per build, 66 MB, and no static release; the standalone binary is fast, published for both architectures and already trusted by the feeds.

decision: How pages read is declared in tables.toml ([site] and [pages.<table>]) and rendered by tad; no repository keeps a renderer of its own. Refined the same day by 2026-11-12-tad-is-text-as-data: presentation stays declared as data, but in the renderer's own file, not in tables.toml, and the renderer leaves tad.
rejected: A renderer per repository (code each must keep, and DuckDB with it in the canon's case).
why: The canon kept its own renderer only for its presentation; declared as data, its seven pages came out identical but for the notice line, and any repository can say how it reads.

decision: tad answers real SQL again: tad sql runs a statement over the declared tables through an embedded SQLite - a query reads them, a change is checked by tad (every row and rule) before the tables are written back in canonical form, as the Python version did with DuckDB. Proven equal on the four repositories' own queries before anyone relies on it. Superseded the same day by 2026-11-12-sql-is-duckdb: the original 2026-09 research had already weighed SQLite and chosen DuckDB.
rejected: No SQL (the rewrite's choice - it left tad unable to answer questions about its own data); GlueSQL (pure Rust, storage as a trait, but younger and a smaller dialect); DataFusion (built for analytics at scale, heavy for this); DuckDB again (a large engine to embed, and the declaration already gives the types).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: the whole point of tad is that it can be used with real SQL; and lab-agent's journal will be tad tables that must be queried. The Rust rewrite had dropped SQL as optional - that was wrong.

decision: tad sql runs on DuckDB, as the original research decided: the declared tables are read into DuckDB, the statement runs, and the tables come back through tad's checks and canonical form; whether DuckDB is embedded in tad or called as its pinned standalone binary (as the phone project's feeds already do) is settled by measuring both on the release build.
rejected: SQLite (weighed in 2026-09, and DuckDB chosen); no SQL (the 2026-11-11 rewrite's mistake).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: SQL was the whole point of tad, researched with prior art before tad existed (why-tad-exists). The 2026-11-12 choice of SQLite contradicted that research, which had weighed SQLite with sqlite-diffable and chosen DuckDB for its native file layout, rich types and measured zero-diff round trip.

decision: tad installs its own SQL engine: tad engine fetches DuckDB's pinned binary for this machine into tad's own folder and checks its fingerprint before unpacking; tad sql uses the one named in TAD_DUCKDB, else tad's own, else one on the PATH. The pin lives in the adapter that owns it and moves with tad's releases.
rejected: A copied install-duckdb script in each repository (copies drift); asking each person to install DuckDB themselves (no pin, no fingerprint).
why: An install script copied into each repository is what drifted before (delivering-tad); the DuckDB adapter owns where its engine comes from.

decision: tad's concern is text as data and nothing else: declare the tables, keep them checked and canonical, and make them easy to create, read, update and delete through files, text tools and SQL. Rendering is a use of the data, so it leaves tad for a small tool of its own that consumes tad, taking the presentation declaration ([site], [pages]) out of tables.toml with it; the four repositories' pages are proven byte-identical before tad drops render. tad grows only where working with the data is inconvenient.
rejected: Keeping rendering in tad (two concerns in one tool, and presentation mixed into the data's declaration); moving it into the observatory's engine (projects would need the observatory to show their own pages).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: rendering, or any other use of the data, is not tad's concern; it was added in the Python days, before there was anywhere else for it. Half of tad's code (1,288 of 2,601 lines) is rendering; ocoeco uses only tad's check. The renderer becomes its own tool, not part of the observatory's engine, because no project may need the observatory to work: a project draws its own pages.

decision: When rendering has left, this repository is renamed tad: it then holds only tad. The names tad-engine and text-as-data-template are artifacts of the vendoring era, when the engine was split out to be copied into each repository - an early, hand-made form of what Rhizoid's cuttings are for. text-as-data-template, which still carries the Python engine, is retired with a pointer once nothing starts from it: a new repository starts with ocoeco init and a tables.toml.
rejected: Keeping both names (they describe how tad used to be copied, not what it is); renaming before rendering leaves (the repository would still hold two concerns).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: tad and tad-engine come from the old era, explored before rhizoid and rhizcut existed; the template mixed rendering in, and the engine was what tad should be.

decision: A release tag is moved only after the change has landed - by land --tag, which confirms the merge first.
rejected: Tagging by hand in the same breath as landing.
why: A job moved v1.0.1 after its change had been refused, so the tag claimed a fix it did not hold; a rule kept in mind failed, so land enforces it.

decision: Projects call the conveyor's reusable workflows, pinned to a version; nothing is copied into them.
rejected: A template repository; copy-paste with care; composite actions alone (they cannot hold whole jobs).
why: snapall and lab-agent carry about 500 lines of nearly identical workflow each; copies drift and fixes do not travel.

decision: The extraction is proven by moving snapall and lab-agent onto the conveyor with byte-for-byte the same published repositories - same URLs, same keys.
rejected: Proving it on a new project first.
why: An extraction that changes what users receive cannot be told from a regression.

decision: 'Nothing changed for users' means the same addresses and key, every signature verifying, and the README's install line installing the new release - not byte-identical packages.
rejected: Byte-for-byte identical repositories (the earlier wording of this decision).
why: Arch packages built twice differ in their timestamps; the byte promise could not be kept and would test nothing a user meets.

decision: Each project keeps its own signing key for now; one key for the whole commons is considered later.
rejected: One organisation key from the start.
why: A single key would change the trust of every existing installation at once.

decision: The conveyor's direction is to build in the project's own Nix environment (the shell.nix the lab machine uses), from Nix's binary cache; the patient retry stays as a fallback meanwhile.
rejected: Only retrying; switching to another single distribution's mirrors.
why: The author asked whether we must rely on Ubuntu's archive; Nix gives one pinned toolchain for the lab and CI, from a more robust source.

decision: A project describes its delivery in one small declaration file; the workflow inputs stay few.
rejected: Workflow inputs only.
why: Inputs grow without limit and are scattered across callers; a file is read, reviewed and checked like data.

decision: The conveyor's scripts live inside its workflows, not as files it fetches.
rejected: A scripts folder checked out at run time.
why: A called workflow does not know which version of itself was called, so fetched files could drift from the workflow; inline, they move together with the tag.

decision: Arch (pacman) and Alpine (apk, for postmarketOS) first, each with a signed repository.
rejected: Debian and RPM repositories first - installation on them stays verified, as today.
why: These are what the lab, the desktops and the phone actually run.

decision: The declaration is read by a typed Rust reader that refuses unknown fields, not by Python inside the workflows.
rejected: Python's tomllib inline (the first version); a shell TOML parser.
why: Shipped code that other projects call: with Python a misspelled field is silently replaced by a default - a bug Rust's types rule out by design. Asked by the author: no Python for new things.

decision: Cutting versions stays with each language's own tool (release-plz for Rust); the conveyor starts from a release tag.
rejected: The conveyor owning versions.
why: Versioning is part of a project's own decisions and tooling.

decision: devlab kernel install refuses a kernel that is not an EFI executable.
rejected: Documenting which file to pass.
why: The bootloader starts EFI programs only; a gzip kernel was lost before it could log a line.

decision: devlab health waits until the phone has been up 90 seconds before checking, saying so once.
rejected: A fixed sleep in every script; checking at once and retrying failures.
why: Every job slept before a health check by hand (7 times); a check read too early fails for the wrong reason.

decision: A listening test runs only with --placed, the word that the microphone is by the phone.
rejected: Un-naming the microphone's file as the safeguard: a trick only its author remembers.
why: The first results came from a microphone being worn.

decision: devlab kernel try waits for a new boot id and reports the outcome itself, judged from the running release, the entry's counter and the timeout log.
rejected: Waiting for the phone to go down and then up (it misfired twice: the try schedules its reboot); leaving the reading to a person.
why: Booting a test kernel and reading what happened was the heaviest manual work (9 times, 54 effort-minutes), and guessing at it cost three reboots.

decision: Test kernels are booted from their EFI image (vmlinuz.efi), and the conveyor refuses anything else.
rejected: Sort keys, a stored default entry, a second boot partition - each checked and ruled out.
why: A gzip kernel was chosen by the bootloader, counted down, and could not start - silently, before any log.

decision: The audio pin driver's function slots for the SoundWire pins follow the phone's own Android kernel (gpio19 swr_tx_data in slot 3, gpio23 swr_rx_data in slot 2).
rejected: Treating the clocks switching off as the cause; changing the macros' autosuspend.
why: A bus clash on the TX bus came right before the codec's timeout; the driver's table disagreed with the vendor's pin description on exactly these pins; corrected, the codec came up on the first boot.

decision: Boots that come up without the sound card are measured over a run of reboots before anything is changed.
rejected: Unmasking the helper service masked for the suspend crash, on a hunch.
why: It happened once in several boots; the audio processor's service channel never appeared. A guess at a cause would be untestable without a rate.

decision: With the SIM in, the modem is examined read-only first; switching the radio on is the only change made, and nothing that calls, messages or uses data happens without the author's word.
rejected: Trying a call or a data connection straight away.
why: A SIM card costs money and reaches people; the phone's state stays known.

decision: The capture failure is not chased in runtime power management.
rejected: Changing the macros' autosuspend or the controller's clock-stop handling.
why: With the bus controllers, macros, codec and SoundWire devices all forced awake, the read failure came at the same moment, the same way.

decision: The right channel is the bottom speaker.
rejected: An earlier 2 dB lean, taken while the microphone was not yet placed.
why: With the microphone at the bottom speaker the right channel read 7 dB louder (-20.4 against -27.6 dBFS; room -85.7).

decision: Where the community's report and our measurement disagree, both are shown side by side; where we know nothing, the report is shown outlined, dated, as reported.
rejected: Hiding a report behind our measurement; filling unknowns as if measured.
why: A disagreement is the most telling part of the comparison - the sensors one may be of our own making.

decision: Telephony is checked in three modes: automatic now (registration; a small download over mobile data), half-manual (the phone calls the author's other phone, the author confirms through the inbox), and fully automatic later (a two-phone stand, or a number that answers with a tone). The number to call lives in a private file on the lab machine, never in a repository.
rejected: Calls by hand without a check; keeping the number in the device manifest.
why: The author allowed data and calls to his other phone, and asked that the checks become part of the test suite so a stand can run them unattended.

decision: Every Rust tool in the commons declares its invocation surface - arguments and environment - with argenv, the commons' own crate: ocoeco, tad, the engine, devlab and tone move from clap, one at a time, proven equal (the same commands and environment behaviour).
rejected: Keeping clap (a second way to declare a surface, and environment read by hand).
why: The author asked whether all our tools use argenv; only lab-agent and snapall did. clap was chosen by default without looking inside the commons first; argenv gives one declared, typed, machine-readable contract for argv and env, readable by agents and by ocoeco.

decision: Every change carries a record made by ocoeco (a changes table in the shared language), the commit message is rendered from it, and ocoeco release consumes the records to set the version, write release notes tied to milestones and backlog, and tag - taking over from release-please and release-plz. The guarantee is at the boundaries that cannot be skipped: land refuses a change with no record, and a CI check on every pull request does the same; a local hook only points the way. Local commits stay free; the record is per change. Refined the same day by 2026-11-11-glimpses: the record is the glimpse, made while the work is fresh; a change is the glimpses it carries.
rejected: Records only in commit messages (lost to squash merges, readable only through git); refusing every local commit with hooks (they fight rebase and amend, are bypassed with --no-verify, and the bypass becomes routine); adopting changesets or Knope as they are (a bump and a summary, tied to nothing else); keeping release-please (prose that drives nothing).
why: The author: data about work goes stale because nothing guarantees it is produced; release tooling writes prose nobody consumes, while ocoeco already knows tasks, goals, decisions and effort. 48% of recent landings produced any data.

decision: ocoeco check reads a project's essence as advice and never fails on a gap.
rejected: Failing the check until every step is served.
why: A gap is the truth about a project, not an error in its data.

decision: Code is changed by structure: whole items replaced with ast-grep, matched by their signature; logic kept outside macros where tools and readers see it; new views and tools added as new files; every edit verified before anything lands.
rejected: Text patches with better anchors; Comby (language-agnostic, less exact for Rust); writing our own rewriter.
why: Patching source by matching text was the heaviest manual work (19 times) and the cause of most failed runs, one of which landed a commit that changed nothing.

decision: Hand-work saturation is measured in effort - minutes weighted by load on Borg's CR10 scale - as well as count; there is no deliberate status: looking, listening and deciding are counted and automatable like the rest.
rejected: Count alone; NASA-TLX's six ratings on every bump (too heavy); exempting judgment from automation.
why: The author's 30 kg box: ten seconds, yet draining. And tests must judge sound and pictures themselves, with no person judging mid-run (jidoka).

decision: The record of work is the glimpse, made through ocoeco at any moment while the work is fresh; ocoeco supplies most of it (what ocoeco note wrote since the last glimpse, the backlog items and milestones they serve, the effort), and the person or agent types a line. ocoeco commit renders a commit from the glimpses not yet committed, with a trailer per glimpse; ocoeco release consumes the glimpses of what has landed. Git depends on ocoeco, never the reverse: a glimpse needs no git.
rejected: One record per change, written at commit time (later than the work, and tied to git); records only in commit messages; hooks refusing every local commit.
why: The author: capture data where it is fresh, while the work is remembered, not sorted out afterwards; and git operations depend on ocoeco, not ocoeco on git. This refines 2026-11-11-changes-are-records, whose record was tied to a change.

decision: Hand-work becomes part of ocoeco's language: a handwork table of atomic actions with counts, recorded by ocoeco hand (match, bump, or ask), shown by the observatory as hand-work worth a tool.
rejected: Logging whole tasks (they never repeat); free-text notes in the session log (they cannot be counted); bumping on any resemblance without asking (silent merging of different actions).
why: Proposed by the author. A board task is many steps and never repeats; atomic actions do. The wording is kept from drifting by the tool, as the vocabulary keeps words from drifting.

decision: ocoeco check names every table a repository keeps beside its exported ones but does not export.
rejected: Exporting every file automatically - some are kept for a project's own use.
why: A device lab's whole backlog and a tool's decisions and log went unseen by the observatory for days; ocoeco note found it by refusing.

decision: The shared language is language.toml, a tad declaration; ocoeco note checks each row it writes with tad's check_row; the shapes kept as Rust constants are gone.
rejected: Rewriting every project's tables in tad's canonical form now (churn in 22 projects, no reader gains); keeping the shapes in Rust (a second declaration language).
why: One way to declare and check tables across the commons: tad's, readable by people and by any tool. A test proved the file said exactly what the constants said before they were removed; ocoeco's own tests pass unchanged.

decision: Hand-work is called manual work everywhere - the table manual_work, the command ocoeco manual, land --manual; every record and bump appends a timed event to manual_events.
rejected: hand-work (less plain); ocoeco did (the person does, not the tool); inventing times for the history recorded before.
why: The author: manual work is the plain word, and with the time kept it can be set beside commits and releases. A command named manual could be read as documentation; the vocabulary defines it, and ocoeco has no documentation command to collide with.

decision: Rows are recorded with ocoeco note, not hand-written per job.
rejected: A per-job script; a general JSON editor that knows nothing of the format.
why: Every job wrote its own script to patch JSON: the same handwork again and again, each a chance to break a table. On its first use the tool found that ocoeco itself exported no decisions.

decision: ocoeco manual without an action opens a list in the terminal (ratatui): type to narrow, arrows, Enter, the usual minutes and load offered.
rejected: A web form (not TTY-first); fuzzy matching on typed text alone (it guesses).
why: Asked by the author: typing an action again is a chore and splits the ledger into near-duplicates.

decision: Research joins the language as its own table (question, found, sources, date); decisions cite it and name the steps they are about; the observatory badges each step with its decisions.
rejected: Sources alone (a list of works says nothing of the question asked); a separate research page with no link to steps.
why: Asked by the author: research should back decisions visibly, beside the milestones and progress they concern, and looking around should be a practice for agents and humans alike.

decision: Any row may be researched rather than live: it cites a research entry and is drawn outlined, with its age and a link; research gains versions (topic, date, supersedes), a refresh horizon, and a place in the attention view when it goes stale.
rejected: Copying outside claims in as if measured; overwriting research on refresh; marking live data (live is the default).
why: Asked by the author, to fill the picture honestly with what others achieved.

decision: Vocabulary becomes part of ocoeco's language: a vocabulary table (term, means, not, see), the shared words defined by ocoeco itself, a project's own words beside them, translated like everything else, and shown in views.
rejected: Folding definitions into the concepts table; a glossary written by the observatory about projects.
why: Asked for by the author, so the work can be spoken about clearly; concepts and vocabulary answer different questions.

decision: Where the whole is weakest right now is where attention goes.
rejected: triage (medical jargon); focus; priorities (a ranking someone sets)
why: What should be looked at next, read from every project - not what is loudest.

decision: An idea a project rests on, with why it matters, is a concept.
rejected: principle (a rule to follow, a narrower thing); belief
why: Distinct from idea (why the project exists) and from vocabulary (what a word means).

decision: A shared process that projects call, not copy, is a conveyor.
rejected: pipeline (CI jargon, and one run); template (copied, the opposite)
why: A conveyor carries any load the same way; you put work on it, you do not build your own.

decision: A lens chosen to stand in the observatory's navigation is curated.
rejected: featured, pinned (web jargon); official (claims an authority it does not have)
why: Says chosen with care, and nothing more; any lens is still found without it.

decision: An owned fork pinned upstream and changed only as patches meant to go home is a cutting.
rejected: fork (suggests drifting apart); vendored copy (a frozen copy, nothing goes home)
why: Rhizoid's gardening word: a cutting is a living piece of the parent plant, grown in your soil.

decision: A choice taken, with why and what was rejected, is a decision.
rejected: ADR (an acronym a reader must be taught); choice (says nothing of the alternatives)
why: The plain word; the rejected options are what make it worth keeping.

decision: Minutes weighted by load are effort.
rejected: cost (money); toil score (jargon); workload (NASA-TLX's wider measure)
why: Effort is the plain word for time and strain together - the 30 kg box.

decision: A project's whole chain on one page is its essence.
rejected: overview, summary (say less, not more); dashboard (numbers, no reasons); at a glance
why: Essence is what a thing most truly is; the page shows why, what, how and now at once.

decision: The daily job that writes down what a project's work produced is its gatherer.
rejected: collector (monitoring jargon); logger; recorder (plain, but breaks the metaphor)
why: One metaphor, kept whole: gatherers in each field, the harvest brought in by the observatory.

decision: The observatory's reading of every marked project is the harvest.
rejected: crawl, scrape (say how, not what); sync; import
why: It brings in what the gatherers gathered; the pair is easy to keep in mind.

decision: The three stretches of a path are horizons.
rejected: phase, stage (imply one ends before the next begins); level (sounds like a score)
why: Horizons are near and far at once - working, perfection and ongoing perfection are all in view together.

decision: Why a project exists, told for anyone, is its idea.
rejected: vision, mission (corporate jargon); pitch (selling); purpose (narrower)
why: The everyday word; a reader knows what an idea is without being taught.

decision: A grand view of a family of projects, declared as a small file, is a lens.
rejected: view (every page is a view - two meanings); dashboard; portal
why: You look through a lens; many lenses can look at the same commons, and anyone may make one.

decision: How draining an action was this time is its load.
rejected: exertion (formal); fatigue (an aftermath, not the act); difficulty
why: Short and physical, as in carrying a load; one number from Borg's CR10.

decision: The file by which a repository joins the commons is a mark.
rejected: manifest (a package's description elsewhere - two meanings); badge (a picture); tag (GitHub topics are only half of it)
why: Short and plain: a mark is something you put on a thing to say what it belongs to.

decision: A step on a path is a milestone, reached only when its evidence exists.
rejected: step (too small to name a stretch of work); goal (aims, not proves); checkpoint
why: The word readers know; the vocabulary adds only the rule that evidence reaches it, not a date.

decision: The mirror that reads and draws the commons is the observatory.
rejected: dashboard, portal, hub (suggest control)
why: One watches from an observatory and changes nothing: the mirror, not the control centre.

decision: The commons' language and machinery keep their own name, ocoeco.
rejected: a descriptive name (it is the name of a thing, not a description)
why: A proper name, chosen by the author: the observatory's ecosystem - the blood and heart.

decision: What a project must reach is its path.
rejected: roadmap (promises dates, a second meaning we do not want); plan; route
why: A path is walked step by step and says nothing of dates - exactly a list of milestones with their evidence.

decision: A repository with a mark is a project.
rejected: repository (says where, not what); module; component
why: The plain word everyone already uses; one repository, one project, one mark.

decision: The look around before acting is research.
rejected: prior art (the sources, not the looking); investigation; due diligence (legal)
why: The everyday word for looking into something before deciding.

decision: Manual work done often or heavily enough to ask for a tool is saturated.
rejected: overdue (blames); hot spot (jargon)
why: The author's own word; it says full - nothing more should be carried by hand.

decision: A work a project stands on is a source.
rejected: reference (also means a pointer); citation (the act, not the work)
why: The word readers know from any citation.

decision: The words a project speaks and exactly what they mean are its vocabulary.
rejected: glossary (a list at the back of a book); dictionary; terminology (formal)
why: A vocabulary is a language spoken - the ubiquitous language of domain-driven design - not a list kept at the back.

decision: What actually happens is work: the backlog, the log, what the gatherers record.
rejected: activity (only commits); progress (a judgment, not a record)
why: Plain, and set against the plan; the Essence page asks of it: what is happening now.

decision: How the steps are delivered and proven are its workings, as in the workings of a clock; a single entry is called by its kind.
rejected: working (unusual as a noun); means (plain, but it would collide with the vocabulary's own means field - one word, two meanings); mechanism (sounds like code only); instrument
why: Workings is everyday English for the parts that make something work. Working as a singular noun is unusual and was the weakest word in the language.

decision: Words are chosen like decisions: a vocabulary entry names the decision that chose it, the decision records the words rejected and cites research; every vocabulary is reviewed this way.
rejected: Definitions without reasons; leaving the words as they first came.
why: Asked by the author: wording is part of perfection. A word is how everyone after us will think about the thing.

decision: A lens's focus is declared as data in its file: parts, each a query over the lens's gathered tables and one line laying out an answer ({name} is that answer's value; {count} in a heading; {today} supplied by the computer). ocoeco focus LENS gathers the lens's tables from this place, or from every place under a root - each row with its star - and runs the parts through tad's SQL engine. The work lens's focus replaces the hand-written board: on every star's main it printed the same 12 lines, byte for byte.
rejected: A language of its own for layout (one line per answer is enough to equal the board; more is added when a lens needs it, not before); formatting in Rust (the hand-written view lenses exist to end); replacing the board before the focus equalled it.
why: The same data, brought into focus (2026-11-12-a-lens-focuses), and proven equal before replacing, as tad's Rust version was. How it reads is now data: changing a word is editing the lens, not the program.

decision: The second face of a lens is its focus, not its showing; ocoeco's acts are glimpse, observe and focus. A lens lets data through and brings it into focus; what is seen is on the fulldome. Shine names no act: it is what a star does by working.
rejected: show and showing; render; resolve; image; project and projection; reveal (each with its reason in the word's entry).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: a lens propagates light, by itself it shows nothing, and showing is a word from another domain. Optics defines a lens by exactly this - it transmits light and brings it to a focus (research the-word-focus). The word also parts two things that showing had run together: the lens that orders, and the fulldome where it is seen.

decision: A lens has two faces: its glimpse takes data in, its showing gives it out. The glimpse says the data's place and relations and how it is entered with ease; so a lens defines the data it needs, and the shared language is no longer written from outside - its tables and relations become the glimpses of the lenses that need them, regrouped, not rewritten. ocoeco glimpse brings all lenses' glimpses together: subcommands and flags declared with argenv, a collision found when ocoeco is built; with no arguments it opens a composed view of them all. The acts are glimpse, observe and show; ocoeco note gives way to ocoeco glimpse. One lens defines a piece of data; other lenses may read it, safely, because lenses are additive.
rejected: The shared language kept as one file apart from any lens; note as the way in (it asks one to know the tables); a glimpse for each table (a lens with several kinds of row has one glimpse with several entries); lenses loaded while running (a place builds its ocoeco with its lenses - the rhizoid way - so nothing is loaded blind).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: the earlier concept of glimpses now has its place - a glimpse is a part of a lens; our database structure had been dictated by us from outside the system, and now fits in naturally; a glimpse also defines how to gather data with convenience - not retyping what already is, not dialling in what the computer can get; collisions are flagged in the making, never in use. It also answers a caution of the same day: a lens need not bring instruments of its own, because the entry follows from the declaration.

decision: A lens's glimpse is its entries, declared in the lens: what an entry is called, the table it fills, what a person is asked for, and what the computer supplies and when - new, always, FIELD changes, FIELD becomes VALUE. The computer knows today and who; what a person gives always stands. ocoeco glimpse alone shows every entry of every lens; ocoeco glimpse ENTRY --id ID --FIELD VALUE makes one, and a field the entry does not have is refused with what it does ask for. Two entries with one name, or an entry filling a table its lens does not define, stop the build. The work lens's first entry is item: since and driver are supplied.
rejected: A language of conditions (three plain ones cover the flow; more when a lens needs them); changing the shape of ocoeco glimpse "what was done" now (every job and every landing uses it: it goes on as before, and becomes an entry of the results lens when that lens gets its glimpse); flags built by argenv in this step (ocoeco's own command line is not on argenv yet: the collision is met at build all the same, by the build script).
why: Not to retype what already is, nor dial in what the computer can get (the author, 2026-11-12). Until now since and driver were typed by hand on every move, and ocoeco note took any field name, so a mistyped one was written as a new field.

decision: The shared language is held by the lenses that need it: the fourteen tables and thirteen relations moved from language.toml and relations.toml into six lens files (lenses/*.toml) - purpose, knowledge, reasoning, work, results, looking back - each saying what it is and which lens it grew from. ocoeco reads its language by putting the lenses' tables together. A lens id used twice, or a table defined by two lenses, stops ocoeco from building.
rejected: Keeping one file and tagging each table with a lens (the lens would still not own its data); checking collisions when ocoeco runs (met in use); rewriting any table while moving it (the proof would mean nothing).
why: A lens defines the data it needs (2026-11-12-a-lens-has-a-glimpse); the structure was dictated from outside in one file. Regrouped, not rewritten: a test holds the lenses, put together, to the language as it stood, table for table and relation for relation. A collision is met in the making, never in use.

decision: There is not one observatory. OCO is the ecosystem - the agreement (ocoeco) and its tools - that lets anyone have one. A constellation has its own fulldome; an observatory is someone's place where the fulldomes they care about come together, and observatories can be brought together, one gathering others. Observer and observatory named one thing: observatory is kept. The author's observatory - where his own constellations come together - is one of many, to be parted from OCO the ecosystem, with which it is mixed today in one organization. Refined the same day by 2026-11-12-places-lenses-acts: observer is kept after all, as the part of ocoeco that observes - an act, not a place.
rejected: One observatory for everyone (a centre the commons would then depend on); a special home of observers above observatories (an observatory gathering others is enough); two words, observer and observatory, for one thing; parting the author's observatory from the ecosystem at once (a careful move, later).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: the point of OCO is that it is not one observatory; anyone will be able to create theirs, and all or some can be brought together to share their views of the sky; OCO as a project had got mixed with his own projects. An observatory that can gather others needs no special home above it - the same thing, nested, as Ostrom found lasting commons to be.

decision: oco- before a name marks a star of OCO itself (oco-agent). -oco after a name marks a place someone made with OCO - a constellation or an observatory alike (linux-phone-oco, marshall-oco). The name says made with OCO; the mark says what kind of place it is.
rejected: A different ending for constellations and for observatories (the mark already says the kind, and a name that says it twice can say it wrongly).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: OCO's stars are named with oco preceding; the observatories others make with OCO end in -oco; the author's own observatory has its organization, marshall-oco.

decision: OCO is three kinds of things. Places, where data lives (git repositories today): a star produces; a constellation is a family of stars that belong together, gathering their data and keeping what holds between them; an observatory is someone's looking, gathering what they care to see. Ways of seeing: a lens - the data it needs, where it comes from, how it is shown - made once and used by anyone; and the fulldome, the outermost lens, the same for every place over whatever it holds. Acts of ocoeco: record (a star producing its data where things are fresh), observe (the observer: gathering from other places, the same at every scale) and show (running lenses). The observer brings data and the names of lenses; since a lens shows the same data the same way anywhere, taking a ready render is a shortcut, not a principle.
rejected: Star and observatory alone (belonging and looking are different claims: one about the stars, one about the looker); the fulldome as one lens beside the others (it would no longer be the whole); the fulldome as something other than a lens (a second mechanism); observer as a second word for observatory (2026-11-12-many-observatories is refined: it is an act of ocoeco, not a place); a lens that must bring its own instruments (a plugin system); observatories gathering only renders (a view of the whole needs the data).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: star, constellation and observatory come from the need for places; without the constellation the relations between projects have nowhere to live; the fulldome is the board taken to its full potential, realized in ocoeco's structure and lenses; a lens, once done, just works for anyone in ocoeco; the observer finds its place in ocoeco as what allows the gathering of gatherings. Sorting the words by kind shows the same shape at every scale (the-same-at-every-scale).

decision: Reflection is an entity of the shared language (language.toml): id, date, by, over, saw, learned, changes, answers (other reflections) and touches (decisions, practices, backlog, research, glimpses - table:id in this project, project/table:id in another). Reflections are written into the data like everything else, so whoever comes next - a person or a machine - inherits the lessons, not only the state.
rejected: Keeping reflections in the session log (a log says what was done, in order; a reflection says what it meant, across a stretch); a reflection per project only (a look back often spans several, so it touches across projects); a separate field for each voice (each voice is its own reflection, and answers the other).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: reflect upon all that was done, as an entity related to the others. A session's lessons otherwise live in a conversation that ends; ocoeco is the place that lasts.

decision: The relations of the shared language are declared as data (relations.toml): which field refers to which table - twelve, among them two that were missing: a decision refining or replacing another (decisions.refines) and work serving a milestone or decision (backlog.serves). ocoeco check verifies every link within a star, and with --root the links into other stars. A field holds several links separated by commas or spaces; table:id names the table; project/table:id points into another star. A milestone's criteria are declared too; what in them is a condition rather than a link to a row (feature:name@level) is passed over.
rejected: Leaving relations to discipline; rewriting existing data to one separator (glimpses use spaces, reflections commas: both are read); putting the relations into tad's declaration now (tad's own references rule does not read lists or table:id yet - it should, later).
why: The fulldome is one sky only if what is connected is truly connected (research the-fulldome-lens-by-lens, ocoeco-as-a-database): about 860 links were kept by discipline alone. On 2026-11-12 one decision refining another was written as prose eight times over.

decision: ocoeco's acts are record, observe and show. Observe replaces harvest and discover. Record stays plain. Show stays plain until the first lens is built and run; shine is kept in mind for it.
rejected: pulse for record (taken by oco-agent's pulse, and it cannot be guessed); shine for show now (it reads as either of two acts); naming an act before touching it.
why: One word, one meaning; a word someone can guess from what it does (research the-words-for-the-acts).

decision: The board is a view over every project's backlog (ocoeco board), never a list of its own. The backlog carries the flow - open, next, in-progress, waiting, parked, done, dropped - and four optional fields: driver (who holds it), next (its next step), since (the day it entered its state), waits_on. The board shows in progress by driver, waiting and on what, next, and what needs attention: more than three held by one driver, in progress with no next step or nobody holding it, nothing moved for a week. oco-agent speaks it when it changes. Refined the same day by 2026-11-12-the-room: the flow of work is one lens of the room, not the room.
rejected: A board kept as its own list (lab-agent's board.json: a second truth); a column per project (the flow is the point, not where an item lives); priorities as numbers or points (the order is the next state, pulled; time is measured as age instead of estimated); hill charts now (worth adding once the flow is lived).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: the board must come from ocoeco's data, with ocoeco and oco-agent developed hand in hand, after the best research. One truth: the backlog is already kept in every project as the work goes; a second list is a second truth that drifts (lab-agent's board was one).

decision: The whole is called the fulldome, not the room, and it has no walls: a part of it is a lens, and what is connected - a decision, its research, the work it caused, the result - is seen as connected. The fulldome shows the story (why a star exists, what it must reach, how, what is happening), time (the sky on any date: the data's own history) and intent, and it is touched and acted in, not watched. What a lens and a render are is not a protocol beside ocoeco: it is ocoeco - the shared language and the mark grow to say them, and ocoeco's tools read, check and write them, so a star follows the agreement by using ocoeco, not by remembering it.
rejected: Room and wall (2026-11-12-the-room keeps its substance; its words are replaced); a render agreement as a protocol of its own (rules to read and remember: the thing ocoeco exists to make unnecessary); a fulldome one only watches (a planetarium's audience: the open commons' must invite).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: room and wall do not fit the whole; a planetarium's dome shows not only constellations but the story behind them, relations, a history, intent; and ocoeco is the agreement and a convenient way to follow it automatically - not principles on paper, a ritual, or a discipline in someone's head. Fulldome belongs with star, constellation, lens, observer and observatory; a dome is one continuous sky, where walls divide.

decision: A board is the room, not a list: the open commons' obeya, where anyone sees the whole. ocoeco's entities are its walls, and a wall is a lens. OCO is described by four words: a star (one idea or project keeping its own ocoeco data), a constellation (stars seen together), a lens (queries and how they are shown, over the same data), an observer (gathers renders, renders nothing of others again); OCO is the home of observers. The flow of work built as ocoeco board is one lens of the room, not the room. A view across stars is a lens of their constellation, rendered once there from the stars' data, so observers still only gather renders; and a render carries a small agreement - its lens, its format, where it starts - so an observer can place it. Lenses declared as data replace three things planned apart: the renderer leaving tad, presentation as data, and the observatory engine's hand-written views. Its words are replaced the same day by 2026-11-12-the-fulldome: the whole is the fulldome, and a part of it is a lens, not a wall.
rejected: The board as a view over the backlog alone (one wall taken for the room: 2026-11-12-the-board is refined by this); a board entity of its own; observers rendering stars' data themselves (a star owns how it is shown, and no star may need an observer to be seen); a framework's ceremonies and score boards; adding words that name no distinct part of the whole.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: ocoeco is the next step, for open commons, of the room where everyone sees the whole - as a principle, a system and an implementation - learnt by seeing and touching, not by cramming; too much had been centred on the backlog; and words are added only where they reflect the whole and make it simpler. The research (the-room) shows the walls are already here, and that the author's four words and the room are one design.

decision: Six meanings, six signs: works, partly, broken or missing, not yet started, not known yet, not applicable. Planned work that has not started is shown calm and grey - never with the red of broken things.
rejected: Reusing the red sign for open backlog items.
why: Red on every planned item painted a project at the idea stage as a failure; like unknown, not yet is not a verdict.

decision: Words are laid out by the browser, never placed inside a drawing: SVG holds shapes only (and fixed-length marks the engine itself makes); every title and label is ordinary text in a cell of its own, shown whole, wrapping inside its cell; a row of cells scrolls sideways rather than squeezing.
rejected: Cutting titles at a fixed length; shrinking the font to fit; adjusting this one path by hand.
why: The path's milestone names were SVG text, which cannot wrap and knows nothing of its neighbours: they ran into each other, and cutting them at a fixed length only hid it until a longer title, a narrower screen or another language.

decision: Every project tells four things about itself, in its own data: its idea (why it exists, written by the project for anyone, as an ordered piece of writing), its path, its workings (how each step is delivered and proven, by which tools, and why we care), and its work. A lens gathers and shows these and writes none of them. The observatory is one more project that tells the same four.
rejected: How we work as one roof - a separate working set beside the projects (decided earlier the same day); the idea as terse cards written about a project.
why: From the author: how we work must not float beside the projects like a random toolbox - it belongs to each project, tied to its goals; and the idea must tell a commoner what this is, in the project's own voice. Shared tools are projects that others' workings name.

decision: The site is a designed static website from tad data - minimal, elegant, no JavaScript - not a tad text page.
rejected: Rendering tad's own pages for the observatory.
why: It is the observatory's visit card.

decision: Discovery is hexagonal; on GitHub the mark is the oco-project topic plus a kind topic, confirmed by oco.toml.
rejected: Code search for oco.toml (slow, rate-limited) as the primary way.
why: Topics are what GitHub's search indexes best: one query finds every marked repository.

decision: The observatory's engine (mark, discovery, harvest, site) is its own repository, in Rust; tad is to be rewritten in Rust with its formats unchanged.
rejected: Extending the Python tad renderer.
why: Sturdier machinery, compiled checks, one toolchain across the commons' tools.

decision: Essence is its own project - the method - beside ocoeco (the language it is written in) and ocoeco-engine (the eye that draws it). It must describe itself with nothing but itself, and be usable: a short guide with a test for each answer, and a measure of how completely any project tells its essence.
rejected: Essence as only a section of ocoeco's specification and a page of the engine; Essence as an essay with no check.
why: Proposed by the author: it gives why and how about how to do why and how. Weighed against the risk of one more box: the method is knowledge neither the format nor the renderer holds, and it is more general than software.

decision: Everything thought, decided and planned is written into the tad structure - concepts, decisions, backlog, session log, milestones - in the project it belongs to.
rejected: Prose documents alone; plans kept in conversation or memory.
why: Nothing may depend on anyone remembering.

decision: How we work is gathered under one roof, the creation-guidelines organization: the canon, the playbook, lab-agent (renamed lab-agent-oco), land and shot (moved from a personal repository), and the practices (moved from the observatory's own design data). Every practice names the tool or check that carries it; the share of practices so carried is its 'how close are we'. It is shown as a curated lens - think, do, tools - replacing the hard-coded page, and lab-agent-oco guide prints the whole working set. SUPERSEDED the same day by "a project, whole": how a project works belongs to each project, not to a roof beside them.
rejected: Leaving practices in the observatory's design data; a page of principles with no tools behind them; a new organization (the roof already exists).
why: Asked for by the author: a working and usable solution set, part of the grand picture, not a manifest. Two practices were broken on the day they were written, both resting on memory alone.

decision: The face uses Project Fluent message catalogs for its interface; projects keep data translations in a standard translations table (with by: human or machine), falling back to the source language; the site is rendered once per language under /<language>/ with identical paths, the root redirecting old addresses; the switcher is a thin line at the header's end naming each language in itself (English · Русский).
rejected: Plain string tables (wrong plurals); translated columns inside source tables; translating rendered HTML afterwards (fragile, no grammar); flags or bare codes in the switcher; switching by script or by the browser's language (no JavaScript, and a reader's choice should be theirs).
why: Fluent gets each language's grammar right (Russian has three plural forms); separate translation rows keep data made by work untouched; prefixes keep paths identical and old links alive.

decision: Grand views become lenses: repositories of their own that declare a family and its views as data; the observatory discovers and renders them all with one engine, curates some into its navigation and lists the rest as discovered. Our views become curated lenses built like any other; linux-phone-oco/docs keeps producing research data and the Linux Phones lens moves to its own repository in its family's organization.
rejected: Views hard-coded in the engine (a bottleneck and a gatekeeper); our views on a privileged path; a free-form template language for views (the vocabulary grows from real needs instead).
why: An observatory of a commons cannot be the only one allowed to look: views as data make the engine a general renderer, open to anyone's family of projects, with no privileged path.

decision: The observatory is a meta structure, tied to no project; its tabs are itself and the grand projects, each with its own views.
rejected: One flat set of tabs for everything.
why: A devices tab made the whole look device-centred; devices are one part of one grand project.

decision: The ecosystem of gathering, chaining and propagation is called ocoeco (observation commons observatory ecosystem).
rejected: Leaving it unnamed; the dashed form oco-eco.
why: It has become an information ecosystem, and deserves a name.

decision: New projects and organizations of the ecosystem may carry -oco in their names - a telling touch, not a requirement. Nothing existing is renamed: belonging is declared by the mark and shown by the topic.
rejected: -oco added to every existing organization, repository, tool and command.
why: Agreed with the author after weighing it: a name that says where a thing belongs helps a person; but identity by name is the mistake Rhizome names, and renaming has real costs.

decision: ocoeco becomes its own repository and the working system from now on: the principle, the formats (tad is the format it speaks), gatherers, chaining, and the mark, discovery and harvest moved in from the observatory's engine, which keeps the face. tad-engine stays as it is, frozen, its formats unchanged.
rejected: Renaming tad-engine in place (its history and users are a different thing); keeping the machinery inside the observatory's engine.
why: The ecosystem's machinery belongs together and apart from the face; tad's name lives on as the format, keeping every existing file valid.

decision: The working practices are tad data in the observatory, and every agent reads them live through lab-agent guide.
rejected: Practices kept only in one agent's memory or in prose files that drift.
why: An improvement made once reaches every agent; no agent depends on its own memory to work well.

decision: Table columns are ranked best first from the data; unknown is shown as unknown and never counted as failure.
rejected: Hand-ordered columns; one 'how close' percentage that counted unknown as zero.
why: The order corrects itself as support grows; a gap in knowledge is not a verdict.

decision: tad is not a template but a rhizoid module (a rhizcut) supplied in every repository, with standard gatherers (CI jobs and hooks reading real files, tests, releases); tad has its own path, shown among the other projects rather than as a top tab.
rejected: tad as a template or a subtree copy; tad as a top tab.
why: Templates and copied subtrees drift and cannot send fixes back; tad is central but smaller than a grand aim like Linux Phones.

decision: Projects are shown against three horizons - working, perfection, ongoing perfection - on the readiness ladder, with milestones whose criteria are measured data.
rejected: A single progress bar; milestones ticked by hand.
why: Overall progress alone loses the reader; three honest horizons show where a project really stands.

decision: Hand-work is recorded on the way every change already goes: land asks for --hand ACTION or --no-hand, and a failure to record stops the landing.
rejected: A reminder nobody must answer; recording after the fact.
why: A ledger is only worth reading if it is never silently skipped; land is the one path every change takes.

decision: The harvest rebases its data onto whatever landed while it worked, and retries the push up to five times.
rejected: Pushing once and failing; force-pushing (would drop what landed); holding landings while a harvest runs.
why: Since land starts harvests, a change landing during a harvest's three minutes rejected its push (2026-11-11 14:45); the harvest writes only its own data/ files, so a rebase cannot collide with what lands.

decision: The lab machine holds an idle inhibitor while the agent serves jobs; it is updated through its package repository regularly.
rejected: Blocking sleep altogether - its owner may still put it to sleep on purpose.
why: It suspended on idle at 03:09 and the agent stayed stuck after waking until a reboot; and it stayed on lab-agent 0.1.39 for days because its package list was never refreshed.

decision: Everything breathes through ocoeco - its language, gatherers and checks - and the observatory stays a mirror: projects produce their data, the observatory reads it, and no project needs the observatory to work.
rejected: Projects depending on the observatory's site or harvest to function.
why: The author's direction that the whole lives through OCO, weighed against the risk of the mirror becoming a control centre and a single point of failure.

decision: No new Python, even for one-off glue: shell orchestrates, Rust carries the logic (rust-script for single files), repeated work becomes a Rust tool; tad stays as it is until ocoeco replaces it.
rejected: Python for throwaway glue; rewriting tad now.
why: Asked by the author: Python's ecosystem is fragile - versions, imports, strings. Measured on the lab machine: a rust-script one-off compiles once in seconds and then runs at once. The deeper cause of failed runs was text patching, answered by structured tools such as ocoeco note.

decision: land starts the observatory's harvest after merging a marked project; the harvest coalesces bursts - one run in progress, at most one waiting.
rejected: Each project's CI dispatching the harvest (a token with rights on the observatory in every project); harvesting every few minutes on a timer (wasteful when nothing changed).
why: Triggering the harvest and waiting for it was manual work done 19 times.

decision: Mechanical rules are enforced by the tools every change passes through, not kept as practices: land moves tags only onto what merged, checks changed workflows with actionlint and commit titles against the conventional form before pushing.
rejected: More practices; more care.
why: The author asked whether such things should be guarded by a tool rather than a mental note; twice in a day a practice did not hold.

decision: Whatever ships or is called by others is Rust; whatever repeats becomes a Rust tool; one-off glue in a job may stay small.
rejected: Python in shipped or shared code; rewriting every one-off line of glue.
why: Python let bugs reach runtime that a compiled language rules out; the record scripts that repeated became ocoeco note.

decision: tad stays the general substrate - a transparent database of text files in git - and is rewritten in Rust; ocoeco is one specific use built on it, and others (Truelink) will be. The wrap-up pass comes first; then tad in Rust is the focus.
rejected: Moving tad's duties into ocoeco and retiring tad (2026-11-11-wrap-up-then-tad, superseded: it would make a general tool specific); hardening tad's Python.
why: The author: tad is simple and general, and proved that a text/file database in git can be accessible, transparent and intelligible; ocoeco is a narrower use of it, and a coming idea (Truelink: facts, their sources and what is drawn from them, so fact-checking can be automated) needs tad too. Python leaves; tad does not.

decision: First a wrap-up pass settling every in-progress item; then the focus is moving tad's duties into ocoeco (declared table shapes, canonical form, documents rendered from data) and retiring tad's Python; phone work continues where it is not blocked.
rejected: Hardening tad in Python; dropping current work mid-way; switching before the board is honest. Superseded the same day by 2026-11-11-tad-in-rust: tad stays general, in Rust.
why: The author: big ideas wait on a backbone that is not Python, and loose ends make the whole hard to read. Making tad's Python pristine would polish what is being retired.

decision: Everything in progress is parked, each item with its resume point, and lab-agent is redesigned first.
